subject: english-language
source_note: Topic structure follows the CCEA GCSE English Language specification. Connections, sequence and prerequisites are expert-authored teaching relationships (exam boards do not publish these).

units.name: Unit 1: Writing for Purpose & Audience and Reading Non-Fiction & Media
units.blurb: Functional writing and reading of non-fiction and media texts (written exam)

units.name: Unit 2: Speaking and Listening
units.blurb: Presentation, discussion and role play (controlled assessment)

units.name: Unit 3: Studying Spoken and Written Language
units.blurb: Investigating spoken language and analysing written texts (controlled assessment)

units.name: Unit 4: Personal or Creative Writing and Reading Literary & Non-Fiction Texts
units.blurb: Expressive writing and reading of literary and non-fiction texts (written exam)

topics.name: Writing for Purpose and Audience
topics.blurb: Writing accurately for a chosen form, purpose and audience with precise vocabulary and correct grammar, spelling and punctuation

topics.name: Reading to Access Non-Fiction and Media Texts
topics.blurb: Reading non-fiction and media texts; recognising language choices and evaluating linguistic, grammatical and structural features

topics.name: Individual Presentation and Interaction
topics.blurb: Presenting information and ideas clearly, using standard English and responding to questions

topics.name: Discussion
topics.blurb: Interacting in a group: contributing ideas, listening, responding and shaping meaning through questions and comments

topics.name: Role Play
topics.blurb: Creating and sustaining roles from real-life contexts and experimenting with language to engage an audience

topics.name: The Study of Spoken Language
topics.blurb: Investigating the characteristics of, and influences on, spoken language and how it varies in different contexts

topics.name: The Study of Written Language
topics.blurb: Analysing characters, themes or genre in literary texts and how writers construct meaning through language

topics.name: Personal or Creative Writing
topics.blurb: Writing clearly, fluently and imaginatively with coherent structure, varied sentences and accurate technical control

topics.name: Reading Literary and Non-Fiction Texts
topics.blurb: Reading literary and non-fiction texts; evaluating how meaning is built and how writers sustain the reader's interest

connections.why: Reading non-fiction and media closely models the language and structural choices students then use in their own purposeful writing
Analysing how writers use linguistic and structural features in Unit 1 is the same analytical lens applied to literary texts in Unit 3
The Unit 1 reading skills (interpreting ideas, evaluating language) extend to literary and non-fiction reading in Unit 4
Controlling form, purpose and accuracy in functional writing transfers directly to shaping voice in personal and creative writing
Audience awareness practised in writing is the same skill applied when adapting a spoken presentation for listeners
The structured, audience-aware talk of a presentation underpins the spontaneous contributions needed in discussion
Interacting and responding to others in discussion feeds the improvised exchanges sustained during role play
The expressive control rehearsed in speaking shapes the distinctive voice expected in personal writing
Understanding how spoken language varies and is influenced sharpens students' own discussion and listening
Comparing the characteristics of spoken and written language deepens analysis of how meaning is constructed in each
Close analysis of literary language in Unit 3 equips students to read and evaluate literary and non-fiction texts in Unit 4
Insight into how writers craft language for effect makes students' own creative writing more deliberate
Reading literary and non-fiction models gives students techniques and forms to draw on in their own personal writing
Evaluating viewpoints in media texts gives students substance and perspective to bring to spoken discussion
Practising deliberate language choices as a writer makes it easier to recognise and explain those choices in others' texts
